name: Macadamia oil

lead: Macadamia oil is pressed from the kernels of Macadamia integrifolia, native to eastern Australia. It is mostly monounsaturated, with oleic acid and an unusual amount of palmitoleic acid, a fatty acid also found in skin sebum. It is used in moisturisers, body oils and hair products for a softer, more supple look.

In products it works as an emollient and fragrance fixative, and its low polyunsaturated content is linked to good oxidative stability. Research covers its fatty acids and stability and dietary palmitoleic acid and blood lipids; trials on skin appearance were not found.

paras: People use it as a body or facial oil, as a hair oil, or as an ingredient in creams and lip products. It is also a cooking oil, and it is generally a daily moisturising step.
Specific topical safety data were not described in the sources. As a tree-nut product it can matter to people with nut allergy.

angle.text: Macadamia oil is a rich emollient used in moisturisers, body oils and hair products, with interest in its palmitoleic acid, which is also found in skin sebum. It softens skin and hair so they look smoother and more supple.

lead: Macadamia oil is a non-volatile oil pressed from the kernels of the macadamia tree, chiefly Macadamia integrifolia, a species native to Australia and now grown commercially.[1] It is mostly monounsaturated: oleic acid is the main fatty acid, and palmitoleic acid, unusual in plant oils, is also present in notable amounts.[1]

It is used as a frying and salad oil and in cosmetics, where it serves as an emollient and fragrance fixative.[1] Research involving it covers composition across cultivars and oxidative stability; studies of palmitoleic acid look at blood lipids and metabolism rather than skin.[2][3][4] No clinical studies of its effect on human appearance were found.
infobox: Clear, light amber, slightly nutty odour[1]

paras: Reference sources give oleic acid as the dominant fatty acid, with palmitoleic acid at roughly a fifth of the oil by one estimate, linoleic acid around 1 to 3 percent and alpha-linolenic acid 1 to 2 percent; exact ranges differ between sources.[1][5] A comparison of oils from 15 cultivars grown in China found differences in composition and antioxidant capacity.[2] Studies on the oxidative stability of culinary oils include macadamia among the oils examined.[4] The low polyunsaturated content is linked to the oil's stability.[1]

In cosmetics the oil is used as an emollient and fragrance fixative.[1] As a food it is used for frying and, more often unheated, in dressings.[1] A Grokipedia entry attributes moisture-retention and wrinkle-reduction figures to cosmetic formulations containing the oil; that claim comes from an AI-generated source and was not matched to a trial in the supplied literature.[5]

Because macadamia oil is a source of palmitoleic acid, studies of that fatty acid are sometimes associated with it. A controlled diet study in hypercholesterolemic men compared palmitoleic, palmitic and oleic acids on plasma lipids,[6] and animal studies examined its effects on lipoproteins in hamsters and on metabolic syndrome in rats.[7][8] A review discussed palmitoleate and glucose homeostasis.[3] These concern dietary intake, not topical use.

The macadamia tree is native to Australian rainforests, and the oil's use as a commercial product follows the spread of cultivation of the nut.[1][5] Grokipedia states that Indigenous Australians used the nuts as food and oil as a liniment, and that seeds were taken to Hawaii in the 1880s; these details come from a single AI-generated source.[5]

No studies found on macadamia oil applied to skin or hair. Registered trials only loosely related to the oil include a study of dietary macronutrients on digestive and cardiovascular health (n=24)[9] and a trial of a vegetable-oil nutritional supplement in people at risk of diabetes (n=25).[10] Their results were not available among the sources, and they do not test topical or cosmetic use.
